Version_comment: Replacing a cargo belt works again, and with it junctions actually take cargo. A cargo belt could never be disconnected: the game identifies a connection by object, and the guard that stops cargo being handed to an ordinary belt was reporting itself rather than the thing it wrapped, so the old connection was never cleared and nothing could connect in its place. Junctions are placed over existing belt, so they hit this every time. Adds two diagnostic log lines to find out why cargo will not enter a junction. Cargo is visible crossing a junction, mergers actually take cargo, and junction track curves like the game's own instead of meeting at right angles. Junctions actually work now. They were drawing nothing, because the new pieces were missing from the list the track drawer walks, and nothing flowed through them, because dragging a line *into* another makes a merge rather than a split and no merger pieces existed - so the placer settled on a splitter facing the wrong way. Both halves of the family are in. Cargo belts branch. Drag a run into an existing one and you get a junction - two or three ways out of one - splitting cargo evenly between the routes, on each level independently. Four new track pieces with models to match. Cargo belts no longer accept loose shapes or fluid, so a space belt or pipe pointed at one backs up at the junction instead of feeding it. A wagon unloader hands over a whole cargo package instead, which also stops a wagon emptying into a cargo belt in a single instant. Rewritten machine descriptions and wiki pages. The wiki pages are rewritten against the game's own entries: no headings, because no vanilla entry uses one; links out to Train Stations, Space Belts, Pipes and Space Levels; and each page closes on the dry one-liner every vanilla entry closes on. The Train Cargo wiki tab is a cargo crate rather than a camera - it was borrowing whichever icon happened to be first in the list. The wiki entries now read like the game's own: concepts are highlighted in the same bold orange vanilla uses, the pages link to each other where one explains another, and the overview and store pages carry a picture of the machines running. The two research nodes show the cargo they unlock rather than a borrowed picture of somebody else's machine. The cargo machines have wiki entries now, in their own Train Cargo section of the knowledge panel: an overview of what packing cargo buys you, and a page each for the belt, the packagers, the unpackagers and the store. Each appears when the research that unlocks the machine it describes does. A loaded cargo belt can be read at a glance again. Its three lane layers now ride abreast on one deck instead of stacked on three, which is what a vanilla space belt does - it fans its layers sideways across the track, not just through it - and what the stacked version could never manage: three decks three units apart made a tower whose top layer stood in front of the two below it. Cargo tools are now bought in the research tree rather than being available from the first milestone: one node for Cargo Machines - the belts, corners, packagers and unpackagers - and a second for Cargo Stores behind it. Both sit in the same research category as the vanilla train station unlock, copied from it at runtime rather than named, because categories are authored per scenario. Cargo is no longer destroyed when a cargo belt, store or packager is pointed at an ordinary belt, a space pipe or a platform's belt port. The connection still forms - the game gives a train station and an ordinary belt the same connector, so it cannot be refused - but the package is not handed over, so the line backs up at the junction instead of quietly losing its freight. Dragged cargo belts now snap to a pipe-tagged output - a fluid packager, unpackager or station - as readily as to a belt-tagged one. The placer could only see the one tag it was typed on, so a fluid machine's output was invisible to it even though the belt connects to it perfectly once placed. Cargo belts and stores no longer draw a red conflict cross while being placed against something that feeds them. They carry a belt connector and a pipe connector at each pivot so one family serves shapes and fluid alike, and the placement preview was marking the unused one as a conflict - over a placement that works. A loaded cargo belt now shows all three of its layers rather than one: the containers were stacked at the spacing the game uses for loose shapes, which for freight this size meant three files drawn almost exactly on top of each other. Cargo belts now set their own layer spacing, and containers sit on their deck instead of half through it. Train unloaders can dock straight against a cargo store or an unpackager with no belt in between - the store packs the loose items itself, the unpackager passes them through. Cargo packagers show a fill gauge per layer on the side panel, so a slow input line no longer looks the same as a jam. The shape and fluid readouts no longer sit on the entrances of cargo machines claiming to be empty - every cargo island now takes part in the prediction graph, so a line shows what is flowing through it and the belt in front of a packager stops reading as a dead end. Cargo belt corners curve the right way round, and the track is drawn as three stacked tiers, one per lane layer, so containers ride on the deck instead of sinking through it. Cargo belts now have their own track model - a channel section with walls and sleepers, swept along a real arc on corners - so they no longer look like ordinary belts. Fixes the cargo store drawing as a bare platform, and cargo vanishing from belts at distance. The machines carry more detail - control boxes, ribbing, stacks, pipe collars and handwheels - and the cargo belt wash now spreads past both sides of the track. Cargo belts run five times slower, cargo turns properly through corners instead of hanging off the outside, and the corner posts and guard rails are gone - the track is washed in colour instead - shaped to the run, so it follows corners. One cargo store now takes either kind of cargo, and a cargo belt holds four containers per layer instead of thirty-two - evenly spaced, lying lengthways along the belt and far bigger. Cargo belts carry both shape and fluid cargo - the separate fluid cargo belt is gone, and the toolbar is one folder instead of two. Fixes two crashes loading an earlier save: the belt state no longer changes the saved blob length, and the old fluid cargo belt ids stay registered so saves that contain them still load. Train unloaders can now feed a cargo belt directly: the belt accepts loose shapes or fluid and packs them itself, so no packager is needed in between - and an ordinary belt feeding a cargo belt no longer silently refuses. Cargo belts now carry one file of full-width containers per layer instead of twelve small ones abreast, and carry corner posts so they are no longer indistinguishable from ordinary belts and pipes. Buffer capacity per chunk is a quarter of what it was, deliberately. Cargo is drawn with the game's own package drawers, so a fluid package shows its fluid's colour and a shape package shows its shape. A cargo store now displays every package it holds - twenty-five per shelf, three shelves - in an open rack with no roof, so you can see what is buffered as you pass. Machine models are no longer red - their colours are sampled from the game's own meshes rather than guessed, and cargotools.uv tunes them live. New toolbar icons for all twelve entries, redrawn in the game's own flat schematic style. On the map, the six cargo belts now draw as real belt and pipe track using the game's own meshes, and the six machines carry generated models. Their colours are still placeholder - cargotools.dumpatlas on the debug console writes the island atlas out so they can be dialled in. Two draggable cargo lines: a belt-tagged one for shapes and a pipe-tagged one for fluids, the latter because a fluid train station will only snap to a pipe connector. Corners chosen automatically. Packagers and unpackagers for both, and detours so every train station accepts cargo packages directly. Adds a Cargo Store that buffers 25 packages per layer, 75 in all, in three independent queues. No lifts yet, so cargo lines cannot cross each other.
Title: Train Cargo Tools
Description: Pack shapes or fluids into train cargo packages and carry them on cargo belts, so cargo can be buffered outside a train station. Stations accept packages directly.
Author: Quinn Bast
